script.opening: "I’m 30 weeks pregnant and most evenings my legs feel really crawly and restless — I get this horrible urge to move them, and it’s worst when I’m sitting or lying down trying to sleep. Walking around helps for a bit. I’m exhausted because it’s wrecking my sleep. What can I do, and is it safe for the baby?"

facts.text: About 5 weeks, getting worse. Both legs, deep in the calves. "Not painful exactly, just unbearable if I keep still." Starts around 8pm and when she lies down; walking or stretching helps for a while. Takes an hour or two to fall asleep; wakes with it at night.

Both legs the same. Ankles "a bit puffy by the evening, both the same". No calf pain, redness or one-sided swelling. No breathlessness or chest pain. No cramps that stop her in her tracks. No numbness or weakness. No back pain.

If asked: saw the midwife yesterday for her 30-week check — "blood pressure and urine fine, baby growing well, she looked at my legs and said the swelling was normal and both calves were fine". Had bloods at booking; "I don’t remember anyone mentioning iron."

Second pregnancy; first baby (Zara, 2) born normally. Uncomplicated so far. Takes a pregnancy multivitamin "most days". Thought about buying a sleep aid from the chemist (an antihistamine). No allergies.
Two coffees a day and tea in the evening. Non-smoker, no alcohol. Works part-time as a pharmacy dispenser. Vegetarian (only if diet is asked). Husband, Imran, supportive.
"I’m tired and a bit teary, but I’m not depressed. I’m just worn out." No thoughts of self-harm.

Tired, warm, a little anxious about the baby. You thought the baby might be pressing on something, or you might be lacking something. Ask "Can’t I have a tablet for the legs themselves?" Accept a plan that includes a blood test and a next step.

ice.ideas: "Maybe the baby’s pressing on something, or I’m lacking something."
ice.concerns: "I’m worried it means something is wrong with the baby." Worried she won’t cope with a toddler and a newborn on no sleep.
ice.expectations: "Something to help me sleep — maybe something from the chemist — as long as it’s safe for the baby."

cues: "Is it safe for the baby?" — reassurance and pregnancy-safe options.
"I was going to get something from the chemist to sleep" — sedating antihistamines can make RLS worse.
"I’m vegetarian" (if diet is asked) — iron deficiency risk; check ferritin.

checkpoints.text: Recognises RESTLESS LEGS SYNDROME from the four core features (urge to move with unpleasant sensation, worse at rest, relieved by movement, worse in the evening/night) and that it commonly occurs/worsens in pregnancy, excluding mimics — especially a unilateral swollen painful calf (DVT, same-day assessment)

TESTS FOR and treats IRON DEFICIENCY (ferritin, FBC and folate; oral iron when ferritin is below 75 µg/L, IRLSSG, international) — a key treatable contributor, especially in pregnancy — with iron and folate replacement

Screens other contributors (thyroid/renal function; medications — sedating antihistamines including OTC sleep aids, antiemetics, some antidepressants; caffeine) and addresses modifiable ones, asking about mood

Manages CONSERVATIVELY and pregnancy-safely (sleep hygiene, gentle exercise/stretching/walking, massage/warmth, reduce caffeine/evening triggers, treat iron) — avoiding dopamine agonists and alpha-2-delta ligands in pregnancy

Reassures that pregnancy-related RLS usually resolves after delivery and seeks OBSTETRIC specialist advice (the obstetric team) for severe/refractory symptoms rather than prescribing standard RLS drugs unsafely
Addresses the exhaustion and the safety-for-the-baby concern, reassures, and checks understanding
Negotiates a pregnancy-safe self-management plan with her, explaining why standard RLS drugs are avoided, so she understands the approach rather than feeling left untreated

Safety-nets and follows up: ferritin/iron treatment and review in about four weeks, same-day assessment for a swollen painful leg, chest pain or breathlessness, mood, conservative measures, specialist advice if severe, and reassurance about post-delivery resolution — iron + conservative care, not unsafe medication

worked.txt: "This is restless legs syndrome — that urge to move with the crawly feeling, worse when resting and in the evenings, eased by moving. It’s very common in pregnancy, it’s not harmful to the baby, and the good news is it usually settles after you’ve had the baby."

"One really important and treatable cause is low iron, which is common in pregnancy — so I’ll check your ferritin, blood count and folate. If your iron stores are low, or even at the lower end of normal, an iron tablet — safe in pregnancy — often improves the restless legs quite a lot."

"I’ll also check your thyroid and review any medications, since some can worsen it — please avoid sleep remedies from the chemist, as many are antihistamines that make restless legs worse. And cutting back on caffeine, especially later in the day, helps. Have you noticed one leg swollen, red or painful? How is your mood?"

"For now, the safest and effective things are gentle exercise and stretching, a walk or leg massage in the evening, warmth, good sleep routines, and reducing caffeine. In pregnancy we avoid the usual restless-legs tablets — both types — so these come first."
"If it’s severe and not settling with iron and these measures, I’ll ask the obstetric team for advice on what’s safe in pregnancy rather than reaching for the standard medications."

"Let’s sort the iron and try these measures, and review how you’re sleeping. If one leg becomes swollen, red or painful, or you get chest pain or breathlessness, that needs same-day assessment. Tell me or your midwife if your mood drops — and remember, it typically eases off once baby arrives."

f.learning: RESTLESS LEGS SYNDROME (RLS) is recognised by four core features: an URGE to move the legs (often with an unpleasant crawling/uncomfortable sensation), worse at REST, relieved by MOVEMENT, and worse in the EVENING/at night. It commonly first occurs or worsens in PREGNANCY (up to about 1 in 5, especially the third trimester) and usually resolves after delivery. Exclude mimics, especially a unilateral swollen painful calf (DVT — same-day assessment in a prothrombotic pregnancy). The key, easily-missed step is to check for and treat IRON DEFICIENCY, a common treatable secondary cause/contributor particularly relevant in pregnancy — check ferritin, FBC and folate, as low or even low-normal iron stores contribute (IRLSSG, international: oral iron when ferritin is below 75 µg/L; BSH 2020 for pregnancy thresholds) and iron and folate replacement often improves RLS. Screen other contributors (thyroid and renal function; medications that can worsen RLS — sedating antihistamines including over-the-counter sleep aids, some antidepressants such as SSRIs/mirtazapine, dopamine-antagonist antiemetics; caffeine) and ask about perinatal mood (NICE NG201) and address modifiable ones. Manage conservatively first — especially important in pregnancy — with sleep hygiene, gentle exercise/stretching/walking, leg massage, warmth/heat, reducing caffeine and evening triggers, and treating iron deficiency, because the usual RLS medications — dopamine agonists and alpha-2-delta ligands — are avoided in pregnancy (owner’s Medwise-reviewed protocol; AASM 2024, international) and should not be reached for. Reassure that pregnancy-related RLS is common and usually resolves after delivery and that conservative measures plus iron are the mainstay, and for severe/refractory symptoms seek advice from the obstetric team on safe specialist options rather than prescribing standard RLS drugs unsafely. The skill is recognising RLS, checking/treating iron deficiency, conservative pregnancy-safe management, reassurance about post-delivery resolution, and caution with medication.

knowledge.guideline: [1] IRLSSG consensus guideline on RLS in pregnancy and lactation, Picchietti et al., Sleep Medicine Reviews 2015 (international) · [2] IRLSSG diagnostic criteria for RLS (international) · [3] British Society for Haematology UK guideline on the management of iron deficiency in pregnancy (2020) · [4] BNF: oral iron preparations and folic acid (doses per BNF) · [5] NICE NG201 Antenatal care (2021) · [6] AASM clinical practice guideline on RLS and PLMD treatment (J Clin Sleep Med 2025) (international)
knowledge.summary: An urge to move the legs, worse at rest and in the evening and relieved by movement, in the third trimester is restless legs syndrome until shown otherwise. Up to about one in five pregnant women are affected, and pregnancy-related RLS usually settles after delivery [1]. The GP’s job is to confirm the four core features, exclude mimics (cramps, positional discomfort, oedema and, above all, a unilateral swollen painful leg suggesting DVT), check ferritin, FBC and folate, correct iron and folate, review drugs that worsen it, and use non-drug measures. The usual RLS medicines are avoided in pregnancy; refractory cases need obstetric advice.

points.t: Clinical, using the four essential criteria [2]: an urge to move the legs, usually with unpleasant sensations; begins or worsens at rest; relieved at least partly by movement; worse in the evening or at night. The symptoms must not be solely explained by another condition such as cramps, positional discomfort, oedema or venous problems. No sleep study is needed for typical symptoms.

Leg cramps (a painful muscle contraction, not an urge), dependent oedema and positional discomfort. A unilateral swollen, painful or red calf needs same-day assessment for DVT: pregnancy is a prothrombotic state. Weakness, numbness in a distribution, or back pain with bladder change is not RLS and needs neurological assessment.

Low iron stores are the key treatable contributor. Check ferritin, FBC and folate. The IRLSSG pregnancy guideline [1] (international) advises oral iron when ferritin is below 75 µg/L in a woman with RLS, a higher threshold than for anaemia. BSH 2020 [3] defines iron deficiency in pregnancy as ferritin below 30 µg/L and gives the anaemia thresholds (Hb below 105 g/L in the second and third trimesters). Oral iron and folic acid doses per BNF [4]; recheck the response.

Sedating antihistamines (often used for sleep or nausea in pregnancy), dopamine-antagonist antiemetics, and some antidepressants can worsen RLS; caffeine, alcohol and nicotine too. Review anything she is taking, including over-the-counter sleep aids, before adding anything.

Moderate daytime activity, stretching or a short walk before bed, leg massage, warm or cool compresses, a regular sleep routine, and mentally engaging activity during enforced rest (a puzzle or reading) [1]. Treat the sleep deprivation seriously: ask about mood, which matters in the perinatal period [5].

Dopamine agonists and alpha-2-delta ligands used for RLS outside pregnancy [6] are avoided in pregnancy. If symptoms stay severe despite iron, folate and non-drug measures, seek obstetric advice; the IRLSSG [1] describes specialist options for refractory cases. Pregnancy-related RLS usually resolves within weeks of delivery; persistent symptoms after birth need reassessment.

model.text: Hello Mrs Qureshi, I’m Dr Shah. Please, tell me what’s been happening.
model.why: Open question; lets her give her story

model.text: I’m 30 weeks pregnant and most evenings my legs feel really crawly and restless. I get this horrible urge to move them, and it’s worst when I’m sitting or lying down trying to sleep. Walking around helps for a bit. I’m exhausted. What can I do, and is it safe for the baby?

That sounds miserable, especially on top of being pregnant. I can hear two things: you need some sleep, and you want to know the baby is all right. I’ll come to both. First, can I ask a bit more about the feeling itself?
model.why: Acknowledges exhaustion and names her worry early

model.text: Yes, of course.
Is it more of an urge to move, or a painful cramp where the muscle goes hard?
model.why: Separates RLS from nocturnal leg cramps

model.text: An urge. It’s not painful exactly, just unbearable if I keep still.
Does it affect both legs? And have you noticed one leg swollen, red, hot or painful in the calf?
model.why: Screens for DVT, a key mimic in pregnancy

model.text: Both legs, and no, nothing like that. My ankles are a bit puffy by the evening, but both the same.
Any numbness, pins and needles in one area, weakness, back pain, or any change with your bladder or bowels?
model.why: Neurological red flags and neuropathy mimics

model.text: No, none of that.
When did it start, and did you ever have anything like it before pregnancy? Does anyone in your family have it?
model.why: Onset, prior episodes, family history of RLS

model.text: A few weeks now, and it’s getting worse. Never before this pregnancy. I don’t know about my family.
What are you taking at the moment, including pregnancy vitamins, anything for sickness, or anything from the pharmacy to help you sleep?
model.why: Drug triggers: sedating antihistamines, antiemetics, antidepressants

model.text: Nothing regular that I can think of. I did wonder about getting something from the chemist for sleep.

I’m glad you asked first, because some of the sleep remedies you can buy are antihistamines, and those can actually make restless legs worse. How about tea, coffee or cola, especially later in the day?
A couple of coffees, and tea in the evening.
Have you been told your blood count or iron was low at any of your antenatal checks?
model.why: Links to antenatal bloods and iron status

model.text: I had bloods with the midwife, but I don’t remember anyone mentioning iron.
How is the lack of sleep affecting you during the day, and how is your mood? Some women find these weeks very hard.
I’m tired and a bit teary, but I’m not depressed. I’m just worn out. I’m worried it means something is wrong with the baby.
What had you thought might be causing it?
I thought maybe it was the baby pressing on something, or that I’m lacking something.
Thank you. Your midwife checked your blood pressure yesterday and it’s in your notes. Could you show me both legs on the camera?
model.why: Video look at both legs; recorded BP; neurological symptoms screened

model.text: (After looking at both legs) Is everything normal?

Yes: both legs look the same, there’s no swelling or redness to suggest a clot, your blood pressure was normal, and you’ve no numbness or weakness. What you describe fits restless legs syndrome: an urge to move, worse at rest and in the evening, eased by moving. It affects up to about one in five women late in pregnancy. It isn’t caused by anything wrong with the baby, and it usually settles within weeks of the birth.
model.why: Names RLS using the four criteria; answers the safety concern honestly

model.text: That’s a relief. So I wasn’t imagining it.

Not at all. And your idea about lacking something is a good one: low iron is one of the commonest reasons it happens or gets worse in pregnancy. I’ll check your iron stores, blood count and folate today.
model.why: Uses her own idea to explain the plan

model.text: If your iron stores are low, or even at the lower end of normal, I’ll start an iron tablet, which is safe in pregnancy and often helps the legs. We’ll recheck the level later.

Meanwhile, things that help: a gentle walk or stretch in the early evening, massaging your legs, a warm bath or a cool pack, keeping a regular bedtime, and cutting coffee and tea after lunchtime. Please avoid sleep remedies from the chemist. Distracting yourself with something absorbing when you have to sit still also helps.
Can’t I have a tablet for the legs themselves?

The medicines normally used for restless legs are avoided in pregnancy, because the priority is the baby’s safety. If it stays severe after we’ve sorted your iron, I’ll ask the obstetric team for advice rather than leave you struggling. How does that sound?
model.why: Explains the medication position without dismissing her

model.text: That makes sense. As long as there’s a next step.

If one leg becomes swollen, red or painful, or you get chest pain or breathlessness, that needs same-day assessment. If you feel your mood dropping, tell me or your midwife. I’ll phone you with the blood results and see you again in about four weeks. What will you try tonight?
model.why: DVT and PE safety-net; mood; follow-up; teach-back

model.text: A walk after tea, no coffee in the afternoon, no sleep tablets from the chemist, and wait for the iron result.
Perfect. I’ll let your midwife know too.

social.t: Severe sleep loss affects work, driving alertness and coping with other children. Ask about practical support at home in the last trimester.
If she works, fatigue may need workplace adjustments; pregnant employees are entitled to a workplace risk assessment.

legal.t: Use medicines only where benefit clearly outweighs risk; check the BNF pregnancy section for any product and record the discussion. Iron and folic acid are standard in pregnancy.
Pregnant women and those who have had a baby in the last 12 months are entitled to free NHS prescriptions in England with a valid maternity exemption certificate.

professional.t: Communicate results and the plan to her midwife; an antenatal anaemia or refractory RLS needs coordination with the obstetric team.
Not every leg symptom in pregnancy is benign: a clear DVT screen protects against anchoring on RLS.

community.t: Midwife and health visitor; national RLS patient charities for self-help information; perinatal mental health services if mood drops.

redFlags: Unilateral swollen, red, hot or painful calf: suspected DVT, same-day assessment
Chest pain or breathlessness: suspected PE, emergency
Focal weakness, sensory level, back pain with bladder or bowel change: not RLS, urgent neurological assessment
Low mood, hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm: perinatal mental health assessment
psychosocial: Worry about harm to the baby
ice: Idea: the baby pressing on something, or a deficiency
Concern: that it harms the baby
Expectation: something safe that helps her sleep

playbook.diagnosis: “This is restless legs syndrome: common late in pregnancy, not harmful to the baby, and it usually settles after the birth.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of it as the nerves’ ‘fidget signal’ getting turned up in the evening. Low iron turns the volume up further, which is why topping up iron often helps.”

management.reflectIce: “You wondered if you were lacking something, and you may be right: low iron is a common reason, so let’s check it.”
management.psychosocial: Treat the sleep loss as real; check mood; involve the midwife and practical support at home.
sharedPlan: Oral iron if ferritin low or low-normal; folic acid per BNF; recheck
Evening walk or stretch, massage, warmth or cool, sleep routine, less caffeine
Avoid OTC sedating antihistamines and other triggers
Obstetric advice if severe despite iron and non-drug measures
safetyNet: Unilateral leg swelling or pain, chest pain or breathlessness: same-day assessment
Low mood or worsening symptoms: contact the practice or midwife; review in about four weeks

pitfalls.intro: This station rewards a clear clinical diagnosis, the iron link, and a safe explanation of why the usual medicines are off the table. Most lost marks come from calling it cramp, missing the DVT screen, or reaching for a tablet.

items.fail: Calling it leg cramps or ‘normal pregnancy aches’.
items.why: RLS is an urge to move, not a painful contraction; the label changes management.
items.fix: Ask the four URGE questions explicitly.

items.why: Pregnancy is prothrombotic and a swollen calf can be misread as ‘restless’.
items.fix: Ask about and look for unilateral swelling, pain and redness.

items.fail: Not checking ferritin, or accepting a low-normal result.
items.why: Iron deficiency is the key treatable driver; IRLSSG (international) treats below 75 µg/L.
items.fix: Check ferritin, FBC and folate and replace iron.

items.fail: Suggesting an antihistamine sleep aid or starting a dopamine agonist or gabapentinoid.
items.why: Antihistamines worsen RLS; the usual RLS drugs are avoided in pregnancy.
items.fix: Non-drug measures first; obstetric advice if refractory.

items.fail: Brushing past ‘is it safe for the baby?’.
items.why: It is her main concern; leaving it unanswered undermines trust.
Iron response and symptoms need review, and clot symptoms need a clear plan.
items.fix: Give DVT and PE advice, phone results, and review in about four weeks.

Urge versus cramp; both legs; DVT features; neuro red flags; onset; medicines and sleep aids; caffeine; antenatal bloods.
Sleep, mood, her idea and fear. Look at legs on video; recorded BP; neurological symptoms.
Name RLS; reassure about the baby; ferritin, FBC, folate; iron if low; non-drug measures; no OTC antihistamines; usual RLS drugs avoided; obstetric advice if severe.

wordPics.fail: Labels it cramps or ‘just pregnancy’; misses the DVT screen; does not check ferritin; prescribes a standard RLS drug or suggests an antihistamine for sleep.
wordPics.pass: Recognises RLS from the four features, checks ferritin and FBC, gives non-drug advice, explains why usual RLS drugs are avoided, and reassures about resolution after birth.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explicitly excludes DVT, treats low-normal ferritin, spots the chemist sleep aid as a trigger, checks perinatal mood, involves the midwife, and plans obstetric advice for refractory symptoms.

avoid.dont: “It’s just cramp, it’s normal in pregnancy.”
avoid.instead: “This is restless legs syndrome: an urge to move rather than a cramp, and there are things we can do.”
avoid.why: Mislabelling leads to the wrong advice and misses the iron link.

avoid.dont: “Try an antihistamine from the chemist to help you sleep.”
avoid.instead: “Please avoid the sleep remedies you can buy: some make restless legs worse.”
avoid.why: Sedating antihistamines are a recognised RLS trigger.

avoid.dont: “Your iron is in the normal range, so that’s not it.”
avoid.instead: “For restless legs we aim for higher iron stores than the usual lab range.”
avoid.why: The IRLSSG (international) advises iron at ferritin below 75 µg/L in pregnancy-related RLS.

SCA_MODELS.text: If your iron stores are low, or even at the lower end of normal, I’ll start an iron tablet, which is safe in pregnancy and often helps the legs. We’ll recheck the level later.

Meanwhile, things that help: a gentle walk or stretch in the early evening, massaging your legs, a warm bath or a cool pack, keeping a regular bedtime, and cutting coffee and tea after lunchtime. Please avoid sleep remedies from the chemist. Distracting yourself with something absorbing when you have to sit still also helps.
Can’t I have a tablet for the legs themselves?

The medicines normally used for restless legs are avoided in pregnancy, because the priority is the baby’s safety. If it stays severe after we’ve sorted your iron, I’ll ask the obstetric team for advice rather than leave you struggling. How does that sound?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains the medication position without dismissing her

SCA_MODELS.text: That makes sense. As long as there’s a next step.

If one leg becomes swollen, red or painful, or you get chest pain or breathlessness, that needs same-day assessment. If you feel your mood dropping, tell me or your midwife. I’ll phone you with the blood results and see you again in about four weeks. What will you try tonight?
SCA_MODELS.why: DVT and PE safety-net; mood; follow-up; teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: A walk after tea, no coffee in the afternoon, no sleep tablets from the chemist, and wait for the iron result.
Perfect. I’ll let your midwife know too.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] IRLSSG consensus guideline on RLS in pregnancy and lactation, Picchietti et al., Sleep Medicine Reviews 2015 (international) · [2] IRLSSG diagnostic criteria for RLS (international) · [3] British Society for Haematology UK guideline on the management of iron deficiency in pregnancy (2020) · [4] BNF: oral iron preparations and folic acid (doses per BNF) · [5] NICE NG201 Antenatal care (2021) · [6] AASM clinical practice guideline on RLS and PLMD treatment (J Clin Sleep Med 2025) (international)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: An urge to move the legs, worse at rest and in the evening and relieved by movement, in the third trimester is restless legs syndrome until shown otherwise. Up to about one in five pregnant women are affected, and pregnancy-related RLS usually settles after delivery [1]. The GP’s job is to confirm the four core features, exclude mimics (cramps, positional discomfort, oedema and, above all, a unilateral swollen painful leg suggesting DVT), check ferritin, FBC and folate, correct iron and folate, review drugs that worsen it, and use non-drug measures. The usual RLS medicines are avoided in pregnancy; refractory cases need obstetric advice.

points.t: Clinical, using the four essential criteria [2]: an urge to move the legs, usually with unpleasant sensations; begins or worsens at rest; relieved at least partly by movement; worse in the evening or at night. The symptoms must not be solely explained by another condition such as cramps, positional discomfort, oedema or venous problems. No sleep study is needed for typical symptoms.

Leg cramps (a painful muscle contraction, not an urge), dependent oedema and positional discomfort. A unilateral swollen, painful or red calf needs same-day assessment for DVT: pregnancy is a prothrombotic state. Weakness, numbness in a distribution, or back pain with bladder change is not RLS and needs neurological assessment.

Low iron stores are the key treatable contributor. Check ferritin, FBC and folate. The IRLSSG pregnancy guideline [1] (international) advises oral iron when ferritin is below 75 µg/L in a woman with RLS, a higher threshold than for anaemia. BSH 2020 [3] defines iron deficiency in pregnancy as ferritin below 30 µg/L and gives the anaemia thresholds (Hb below 105 g/L in the second and third trimesters). Oral iron and folic acid doses per BNF [4]; recheck the response.

Sedating antihistamines (often used for sleep or nausea in pregnancy), dopamine-antagonist antiemetics, and some antidepressants can worsen RLS; caffeine, alcohol and nicotine too. Review anything she is taking, including over-the-counter sleep aids, before adding anything.

Moderate daytime activity, stretching or a short walk before bed, leg massage, warm or cool compresses, a regular sleep routine, and mentally engaging activity during enforced rest (a puzzle or reading) [1]. Treat the sleep deprivation seriously: ask about mood, which matters in the perinatal period [5].

Dopamine agonists and alpha-2-delta ligands used for RLS outside pregnancy [6] are avoided in pregnancy. If symptoms stay severe despite iron, folate and non-drug measures, seek obstetric advice; the IRLSSG [1] describes specialist options for refractory cases. Pregnancy-related RLS usually resolves within weeks of delivery; persistent symptoms after birth need reassessment.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; lets her describe the sensation and the sleep impact before narrowing.
Exhaustion, daytime function, perinatal mood and support.
Picks up her plan to buy a sleep aid and asks about antenatal blood results.
Idea (baby pressing or lacking something), concern (harm to the baby), expectation (relief she can safely use).
Looks at both legs on video, uses the recorded BP, screens neurological symptoms; ferritin, FBC and folate.
RLS versus leg cramps, oedema, positional discomfort, neuropathy and DVT.
Unilateral swollen painful leg (DVT), neurological signs, and perinatal mood.
Restless legs syndrome named from the four criteria, linked to pregnancy and iron.
Ferritin-guided iron, non-drug measures, caffeine and antihistamine avoidance; explains why usual RLS drugs are avoided.
Folate and anaemia addressed; midwife informed; obstetric advice if refractory.
Same-day advice for DVT or PE symptoms; results by phone; review in about four weeks; teach-back.

social.t: Severe sleep loss affects work, driving alertness and coping with other children. Ask about practical support at home in the last trimester.
If she works, fatigue may need workplace adjustments; pregnant employees are entitled to a workplace risk assessment.

legal.t: Use medicines only where benefit clearly outweighs risk; check the BNF pregnancy section for any product and record the discussion. Iron and folic acid are standard in pregnancy.
Pregnant women and those who have had a baby in the last 12 months are entitled to free NHS prescriptions in England with a valid maternity exemption certificate.

professional.t: Communicate results and the plan to her midwife; an antenatal anaemia or refractory RLS needs coordination with the obstetric team.
Not every leg symptom in pregnancy is benign: a clear DVT screen protects against anchoring on RLS.

community.t: Midwife and health visitor; national RLS patient charities for self-help information; perinatal mental health services if mood drops.

redFlags: Unilateral swollen, red, hot or painful calf: suspected DVT, same-day assessment
Chest pain or breathlessness: suspected PE, emergency
Focal weakness, sensory level, back pain with bladder or bowel change: not RLS, urgent neurological assessment
Low mood, hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm: perinatal mental health assessment
psychosocial: Worry about harm to the baby
ice: Idea: the baby pressing on something, or a deficiency
Concern: that it harms the baby
Expectation: something safe that helps her sleep

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station rewards a clear clinical diagnosis, the iron link, and a safe explanation of why the usual medicines are off the table. Most lost marks come from calling it cramp, missing the DVT screen, or reaching for a tablet.

items.fail: Calling it leg cramps or ‘normal pregnancy aches’.
items.why: RLS is an urge to move, not a painful contraction; the label changes management.
items.fix: Ask the four URGE questions explicitly.

items.why: Pregnancy is prothrombotic and a swollen calf can be misread as ‘restless’.
items.fix: Ask about and look for unilateral swelling, pain and redness.

items.fail: Not checking ferritin, or accepting a low-normal result.
items.why: Iron deficiency is the key treatable driver; IRLSSG (international) treats below 75 µg/L.
items.fix: Check ferritin, FBC and folate and replace iron.

items.fail: Suggesting an antihistamine sleep aid or starting a dopamine agonist or gabapentinoid.
items.why: Antihistamines worsen RLS; the usual RLS drugs are avoided in pregnancy.
items.fix: Non-drug measures first; obstetric advice if refractory.

items.fail: Brushing past ‘is it safe for the baby?’.
items.why: It is her main concern; leaving it unanswered undermines trust.
Iron response and symptoms need review, and clot symptoms need a clear plan.
items.fix: Give DVT and PE advice, phone results, and review in about four weeks.
